subject: Climate & Environment
title: Ozone Layer vs. Greenhouse Gases
description: A fast breakdown of Ozone Layer vs. Greenhouse Gases for builders.

hook.text: People often confuse the ozone hole with climate change. They are two separate problems.

buildup.text: The ozone layer blocks ultraviolet radiation from the Sun high in the stratosphere.

discovery.text: CFCs from spray cans destroyed ozone molecules. The 1987 Montreal Protocol banned them.

twist.text: Greenhouse gases warm the surface but actually cool the stratosphere where ozone lives.

climax.text: The ozone layer is healing because the world acted fast. Climate change hasn't had that luck.

punchline.text: We fixed one sky problem. The bigger one is still waiting.

quiz.question: What international treaty helped heal the ozone layer?

details.summary: The ozone layer in the stratosphere protects life from ultraviolet radiation, while greenhouse gases in the lower atmosphere trap heat. Ozone depletion and global warming are different problems caused by different chemicals, though some interactions exist.
details.whyItMatters: Confusing the ozone hole with climate change is one of the most common public misconceptions. Clarity on their differences helps interpret both problems correctly.
takeaways: Ozone depletion is caused by CFCs, not by CO2
The Montreal Protocol successfully addressed ozone destruction
Some ozone-depleting substances are also greenhouse gases

faq.question: Does the ozone hole contribute to global warming?
faq.answer: Ozone depletion has a small cooling effect on the stratosphere and mixed effects on surface temperatures over Antarctica. The bigger warming connection is that CFC replacements, HFCs, are potent greenhouse gases being addressed by the Kigali Amendment.

faq.question: Why was the ozone problem solved faster than climate change?
faq.answer: CFCs had clear industrial substitutes, came from a limited number of manufacturers, and the Montreal Protocol provided a straightforward phase-out. CO2 comes from virtually all economic activity, making the transition far more complex and politically difficult.
